strength: It spots the real issue: the top 5 matte shades, not the whole matte line, need the cash, while liquid and glitter should get no PO.
mistake: It assumes the held crushed-carton units are already inside the 9,100 top-5 stock, so it creates a stockout gap that the re-cartoning fix should largely avoid if those units are additional.
to10: Fix the held-stock assumption, show top-5 stock rising to about 13,000 after re-cartoning, and adjust the stockout messaging and buffers around that.

strength: It gives a tight cash plan with good supporting math, including the draft’s failure, the sale-week uplift, and the cash tied up in slow stock.
mistake: It also treats the held top-5 lipsticks as already counted in the 9,100 units, which makes the hero-shade stockout look unavoidable when the warehouse fix should bridge most of it.
to10: Correct the re-cartoning stock position, give a clearer sell-through floor for glitter clearance, and make the action plan less conditional.

strength: It correctly exposes that PMax is unprofitable without brand, puts the price-mismatch feed fix first, and gives a budget split that adds to $240,000 with profit math.
mistake: The reserve/unspent-budget setup and some PMax controls like 'feed-only' and keyword negatives need small practical caveats so the team does not expect perfect control inside PMax.
to10: Tighten it under the word limit, make the PMax implementation language more platform-exact, and add one or two more ready-to-paste title/ad examples for bags and flats.

strength: It is very clear, gets the core diagnosis right, and puts the feed fix, brand exclusion, bags budget and winning non-brand terms in the right order.
mistake: The forecast leans optimistic, especially assuming brand search can keep about $455,000 of value on $18,000 spend and PMax can quickly rise above its current non-brand 2.03 ROAS.
to10: Ground the forecast in a more cautious range, remove placeholders from title patterns, and give firmer stop/move rules for weeks two to four.

strength: It correctly spots the three real levers: warehouse-exit dispatch emails, bra fit finder visibility, and one-step size swaps instead of refund-first returns.
mistake: It does not include the proactive day-3 update, even though 62% of WISMO tickets arrive on days 3 to 5.
to10: Add the day-3 reassurance message, tighten the rollout around that ticket spike, and be slightly more cautious about assuming fit finder users will keep the full 19-point return-rate gap.

strength: It directly attacks the self-made day-3 to day-5 WISMO spike, the hidden fit quiz, and the refund-biased portal with copy and numbers that fit the brief.
mistake: A few message details need light operational checking, such as whether 'we're packing your order now' and 'your parcel is with courier now' are always true at those trigger points.
to10: Make the trigger wording fully operationally safe and add a slightly clearer split between cost savings and sales retained from swaps.

strength: It spots the switched-off pause as the main win, removes wasteful discounts, and gives the team a compliant one-screen flow with usable copy and working maths.
mistake: The uplift range and the assumed performance of the annual-plan switch and reminder are a bit hand-wavy, so I would want those tightened before using the forecast externally.
to10: Tighten the forecast ranges and test assumptions, especially for the annual switch and reminder paths, while keeping the same flow.

strength: It gives a buildable one-screen flow with mostly good segmentation, strong copy, correct core counts, and a clear testing/logging plan.
mistake: It adds a 50% discount for switchers with no evidence that price is the issue, then counts that assumed save in the upside.
to10: Remove or separately test the switcher discount, keep discounts out of unsupported paths, and make the revenue model reflect only proven or clearly ranged assumptions.

strength: It catches the three biggest removable causes, writes usable answer-first articles, changes the right in-app links, and shows conservative ticket-saving working with correct numbers.
mistake: The restore article includes visible 'Search words' text and assumes exact app labels/restore behaviour that should be checked before publishing.
to10: Hide the search terms as metadata, verify the exact restore and settings labels across platforms, and add the currency article brief for week 2.

strength: It is tightly focused on the main ticket drivers and gives clear, publishable drafts with good in-app link fixes and a reasonable savings estimate.
mistake: It invents some product behaviour and risky claims, especially 'nothing is lost for good', and the proposed merge of the already-working payment article is not well justified.
to10: Remove unsupported claims, skip the low-value payment merge, verify platform steps, and make the forecast a clearer range rather than one headline number.

strength: It makes the right call on keeping 30%, shows the lifetime and break-even maths cleanly, and puts the top-20 creator educators, 90-day window, and payout fixes first.
mistake: The free Podia plan is counted against the perk budget at retail value, which may not match true budget cost, and the Day 30 payout timing may need a tighter finance check.
to10: Tighten the perk-cost assumptions and add one or two concrete partner content examples using Renee/Kwame language.

strength: It gives a strong straight answer against the 20% cut, catches the tracking-window problem, and uses the key lifetime-value maths well.
mistake: The 40% Partner tier adds a meaningful new commission cost on top of the $40,000 perk plan, while the cost case is a bit too soft and the 'free Podia account at no cost' claim is not really true.
to10: Keep the top-tier rewards mostly in service, access, content funds, faster payouts, and 90-day credit rather than matching the rival's 40% rate unless the added commission cost is fully modelled and capped.

strength: It catches the real issue fast: top 5 matte shades will run out before the sale, so it prioritises re-cartoning and a rush PO while cutting zero-value orders on slow stock.
mistake: It says the 9,100 top-5 units are 'counting the held ones' and then projects a stockout gap from that base, which misreads the hold stock and weakens the timing logic around the early-December gap.
to10: Use the held-stock math cleanly throughout, tighten the stockout date and pre-order timing, and keep the same cash-disciplined ordering plan.

strength: It is built on the actual constraint: it puts almost all cash into the top 5 matte shades, starts re-cartoning on Monday, avoids dead-stock reorders, and gives a dated action plan the ops lead can run.
mistake: The palette disposal idea on 1 February via a clearance buyer is a bit speculative and less grounded than the rest of the plan.
to10: Add one tighter customer-facing back-in-stock line in brand voice and show the top-5 rush/standard coverage math a touch more explicitly by date.

strength: It finds the real problem fast: non-brand Google is below break-even, the pointed flat feed issue is urgent, and it gives a concrete reallocation with week-one actions.
mistake: It includes a few risky or questionable platform moves and one awkward budget approach, especially 'reserve' that may stay unspent even though the brief says to split the full $240,000 next month.
to10: Tighten the Google Ads mechanics, make the budget fully deployable to exactly $240,000 without ambiguity, and remove the weaker assumptions around PMax controls.

strength: It cleanly takes apart the headline 4.0 ROAS against the 2.5 break-even, puts the feed fix first, and gives a usable 30-day budget and execution plan tied to the data.
mistake: Its forecast is a bit optimistic, especially the implied brand search efficiency and overall upside after the restructure.
to10: Give a more conservative forecast range with clearer working on the brand and PMax assumptions, while keeping the same practical plan.

strength: It finds the three real levers in this business and turns them into a practical 60-day plan with usable copy, portal changes and sensible low-to-high ranges.
mistake: It overstates the retained-sales upside from swaps with a headline figure that is too generous for the stated refund-share change and could mislead prioritisation.
to10: Tighten the swap revenue math, explicitly include the post-delivery bra-fit help as a measured lever, and keep every forecast fully traceable to the assumptions.

strength: It clearly identifies the silence before courier scan as the fastest ticket win and gives mostly strong, on-brand copy with a sensible build order.
mistake: It misses the owner's hoped-for day-3 reassurance message, replaces it with a late-only message, and its projected totals and savings do not fully tie back to the stated assumptions.
to10: Add the proactive day-3 update, include a dedicated post-delivery first-bra fit message, and fix the forecast table so every number reconciles cleanly.

strength: It turns the data into a buildable one-screen flow with the paused winner restored and reason-matched saves instead of one blunt discount.
mistake: It gives the 50% discount to switchers with no evidence, and its revenue math is shaky because it counts discounted saves and some annual-switch value inconsistently.
to10: Tighten the maths and replace the unsupported switching-app discount with a cleaner exit or tested alternative while keeping the same strong screen-level detail.

strength: It catches the core business truth that the pause is the real lever, says to rebuild it first, and avoids wasting discounts on people likely to return anyway.
mistake: It claims a subscriber range that is not well supported by the stated assumptions, and it is lighter on exact per-reason post-action copy than the owner asked for.
to10: Show fully consistent working for the base, upside and downside cases and add the exact confirmation copy for each non-cancel action.

strength: It prioritises the highest-leverage fixes from the data and gives a sensible low-to-high ticket reduction range with clear working.
mistake: The deleted-expense article invents a restore flow in Activity that the brief never confirms, which is a risky factual miss in ready-to-publish help content.
to10: Verify the product steps and labels, especially restore/undelete, and add the missing currency article plan with the same level of specificity.

strength: It spots the key drivers well, especially Simplify debts, unfound delete searches, app-store refunds, and the chance to improve contextual help links.
mistake: It adds unsupported product claims and actions—web undelete, history showing every change, and a merge recommendation—so I could not trust it to publish without checking line by line.
to10: Remove invented functionality, stick to changes supported by the brief, and give a more disciplined priority list focused on what one writer can ship in two weeks.

strength: It makes the right call against the 20% cut with clean lifetime-value maths, then turns the real levers in this programme: the top 20, the 90-day window, and payouts.
mistake: It slightly overstates confidence on implementation timing, especially making the first payout under the new schedule by day 30 without noting systems risk more clearly.
to10: Add one short line on how existing lifetime referrals are grandfathered so the promise of 'for life' is protected in practice as well as principle.

strength: It clearly says not to cut to 20% and correctly spots that the real fixes are tracking window and payout speed.
mistake: It proposes a 40%-for-12-month top tier without solid cost logic, and its cost maths are shaky enough to change the decision on tiers and budget.
to10: Keep the 30% base, drop the expensive rate uplift, and rebuild the tier around perks, faster payouts, and named support with accurate costings tied to the top 20.

strength: It gives an actionable Monday PO plan inside the ₹1.2 crore cash cap and correctly stops orders for liquid lipstick, glitter palettes and the slow matte shades.
mistake: It misreads the held lipstick stock, so it wrongly says a top-5 shade stockout gap is unavoidable instead of showing that re-cartoning lifts top-5 stock to about 13,000 units and bridges to the rush delivery.
to10: Fix the held-stock assumption and rebuild the top-5 availability dates so the re-cartoning job is shown as the cheap fix that prevents the pre-sale stockout.

strength: It is clear, decisive and commercially focused, with the right cash allocation to top-5 matte shades plus practical moves for artists, palettes and honest customer messaging.
mistake: It also treats the 3,900 held top-5 units as part of the 9,100 on hand, which creates a false 1–8 December stockout gap and understates the value of re-cartoning.
to10: Correct the held-stock math, update the dates to show top-5 stock lasting to the rush arrival, and keep the same clear PO table and customer-facing actions.

strength: It correctly takes apart the blended 4.0 ROAS, identifies PMax brand dependency and the feed disapproval as the first fix, then moves budget toward bags, washable and comfort terms.
mistake: It is a bit overlong and the reserve/unspent-budget framing slightly conflicts with the request to split the full $240,000 for the month.
to10: Tighten it under the word limit and make the reserve rule a clearer reallocation plan so the full $240,000 is actively assigned unless performance fails.

strength: It is very clear, numerically sound, and puts the price mismatch and PMax brand issue in the right order against the 2.5 break-even ROAS.
mistake: It raises bags Shopping without clearly excluding bags from PMax, and its forecast depends on an optimistic brand transfer and PMax recovery.
to10: Add the PMax product exclusions for bags, make the forecast more conservative, and give firmer week-two-to-four cut and scale rules.

strength: It uses the actual return, fit finder and ticket data well, with clear projections and ready-to-send copy.
mistake: It misses the key day-3 proactive delivery update, even though most WISMO tickets arrive between days 3 and 5.
to10: Add a day-3 'still on track' message and soften any delivery wording that sounds too certain.

strength: It tackles the exact three drivers in the data: silent delivery days, low fit quiz use, and the refund-biased portal.
mistake: Pre-selecting swap for size returns is a little aggressive; I would prefer swap first but no option pre-selected.
to10: Keep the same plan but make the portal choice neutral, add preview text for every email, and slightly soften fit language like 'spilling over.'

strength: It turns the strongest data signal into the main save by bringing back the 1-month pause, and it gives product-ready copy for each reason path.
mistake: It keeps an unproven 50% discount for people switching apps and counts that as upside, when the brief points away from discount-led saving.
to10: Remove or test-gate the switching-app discount, tighten the revenue assumptions around discounted users, and make the pause the clear first build priority.

strength: It clearly acts on the main signals: restore the pause, stop wasting discounts on trip completers, move price-sensitive monthly users to annual, and treat lack of progress as a reminder problem.
mistake: It overstates the billing issue by saying the new billing system cannot do pause yet, and it lacks full confirmation copy for people who accept save offers.
to10: Add exact done-state copy for pause, annual switch and reminder acceptance, and soften the billing claim to match the data given.

strength: It acts on the main signals in the data: Simplify debts in the balance article, findability for deleted expenses, and Apple/Google refunds first.
mistake: The forecast uses confident single-point assumptions and adds some lower-priority work, like merging the payment article, that is not clearly needed.
to10: Make the ticket forecast a clearer low-to-high range and remove or defer the payment-article merge so the two-week plan stays tighter.

strength: It gives a clear, conservative ticket-saving range with correct working and puts the right three problems first.
mistake: It proposes a new Simplify debts article rather than fully rewriting the high-traffic article that is already failing, and the visible 'Search words' line is not ready customer-facing copy.
to10: Rewrite the existing 'How balances work' article in full, add hidden search terms rather than publishing them in the article, and include the currency link once live.

strength: It makes the right call against the 20% cut with the lifetime maths, then focuses the plan on the top creator-educator partners and the credit-window/payout fixes.
mistake: The Day 30 payout item is a bit too neat operationally, since a 30-days-after-month-end payout schedule may not produce a real first payout within the first 30 days.
to10: Add a small day-90 scorecard and tighten the payout transition timing so finance and the partner manager can run it without interpretation.

strength: It clearly proves why the 20% cut is risky and gives a strong 90-day window, payout, rules and review plan.
mistake: The 40% Partner tier and free accounts add cost and complexity that are not fully controlled inside the $40,000 perk budget or the one-manager constraint.
to10: Keep the Partner tier reward mostly in managed perks and service, or cap the 40% tier tightly with a clearer cost ceiling and eligibility limit.

strength: It spots the real issue fast: the top 5 matte shades, the re-cartoning fix, and the need to stop ordering by current stock mix.
mistake: It includes a likely impossible 8,000-unit foundation order across only 4 shades despite the 2,000-per-shade minimum and no shade-level proof that four shades need that much.
to10: Tighten the unit math on foundation and kohl, and make the customer message and sale timing fully consistent with the stock gap dates.

strength: It uses the owner’s actual constraint set well: rush and standard orders for the top 5 matte shades, no money wasted on slow stock, and a practical cash-safe action plan.
mistake: It still leaves a little homework by using a conditional reserve rule and by assuming a 'Night-out kit' concept without proving channel and customer fit.
to10: Turn the reserve into a final yes-or-no order decision and tighten a couple of projected quantities so every line is fully locked for Monday execution.

strength: It takes apart the 4.0 ROAS properly, shows non-brand is below the 2.5 break-even, and turns that into a concrete reallocation and week-one plan.
mistake: It includes a few risky or questionable platform moves, especially suggesting PMax negative keywords and removing image/video assets, and its reserve logic implies some budget may go unspent despite the brief saying to split the full $240,000 next month.
to10: Tighten the platform-specific recommendations, make every dollar of the $240,000 allocation operationally committed, and keep the strong profit math and feed-first prioritization.

strength: It nails the main business story fast: brand is masking weak non-brand performance, the feed issue is urgent, and the winners to fund are bags plus washable and comfort intent.
mistake: Its forecast is too optimistic and leans on shaky assumptions, especially a very high brand-search ROAS after shifting PMax brand traffic over, which makes the expected gains look less grounded.
to10: Keep the clarity and prioritization, but show more conservative worked forecasts tied directly to the given numbers and sharpen the budget logic for PMax and reserve.

strength: It nails the three real levers in the data—silent dispatch gap, bra fit, and a refund-biased portal—and turns them into a practical 60-day plan with usable copy and sensible ranges.
mistake: It counts the portal impact only as 'sales kept' and leaves the total savings view slightly muddled, with one or two estimates that should be tightened before being used in a board discussion.
to10: Tighten the commercial math around swaps versus refunds and add a clearer expected range for the post-delivery bra messages, then it would be excellent.

strength: It is clear, owner-friendly, and correctly puts the cheapest highest-impact move first: fixing the dispatch silence that creates most WISMO tickets.
mistake: It misses the owner's hoped-for day-3 reassurance message and instead sends a day-5 late message, so it addresses the problem later than the data suggests and leaves ticket reduction on the table.
to10: Add the proactive day-3 update, include a more targeted first-time bra fit-support flow, and tighten the projections so the expected outcomes and savings fully reconcile.

strength: It spots the highest-value move correctly: bring back the tested 1-month pause for 'I don't have time' and stop wasting discounts on people likely to return anyway.
mistake: Its revenue math is too rough in places, especially valuing the new flow at full £9 for some kept users while also saying 12-month switchers are worth £4.95, and the range is weakly supported.
to10: Tighten the financial model so every kept group is valued consistently and show a simple first-month test plan with exact success metrics.

strength: It gives a buildable single-screen flow with clear copy and correctly brings back the pause for the 'no time' group.
mistake: It keeps a 50% discount for 'switching apps' without evidence, which goes against the data signal to stop broad discounting and weakens both the strategy and the economics.
to10: Remove the unsupported discount path, align every offer to the evidence in the brief, and clean up the valuation logic and segment math.

strength: It spots the three biggest, cheapest wins from the data and turns them into a clear order with usable in-app link changes and a worked ticket forecast.
mistake: It publishes a restore flow that the brief never proves exists, so the 'undo delete' article is risky and could be wrong in a way that changes decisions.
to10: Ground every step in verified product behavior, especially delete/restore, and keep the same prioritisation and quantified forecast.

strength: It prioritises the highest-leverage fixes from the actual ticket drivers and gives a more honest forecast range with working the owner can defend.
mistake: It says to publish three articles this week and does not deliver the currency article, even though it rightly identifies that gap.
to10: Add the missing third top-priority article set in full for the currency gap or make crystal clear why the top three excludes it, while keeping the same disciplined, evidence-led plan.

strength: It sees the real levers in this programme: keep 30%, fix the 30-day window and payouts fast, and put the one manager and perk budget on the top creator-educator partners.
mistake: It slightly overstates one comparison by saying a referred customer brings '$44 more than a customer who found us alone' without allowing for any acquisition cost on non-referred customers, so the true advantage is at least that, not exactly that.
to10: Tighten that one comparison and add one sentence on how to handle grandfathering if any term changes later so the 'for life' promise stays crystal clear.

strength: It gives a clear no to the 20% cut and correctly centres the window and payout problems that partners actually complain about.
mistake: It introduces a 40%-for-12-months partner tier with faulty cost maths and a likely conflict with the existing 'for life' promise, which makes the core recommendation risky.
to10: Keep the rate structure simple and defensible, fix the year-one cost calculation, and focus the spend on top-partner perks instead of changing commission in a way that adds cost and confusion.

strength: It catches the main issue: rush the top 5 matte shades, re-carton held stock first, stop ordering slow matte shades, liquid lipstick and glitter palettes, and stay inside the cash limit.
mistake: It assumes the held top-5 units are included in the 9,100 on hand, so it creates an avoidable out-of-stock gap and says the gap cannot be closed.
to10: Correct the held-stock treatment so re-cartoning lifts top-5 stock to about 13,000 units and aligns the customer/restock plan around avoiding the pre-sale stockout.

strength: It gives a clean Monday-ready order plan with costs, landing dates, reserve cash, demand logic and no spend on the overstocked lines.
mistake: It makes the same held-stock mistake, saying the top 5 shades will sell out whatever we do when the re-cartoning should materially close that gap.
to10: Fix the re-cartoning math, make the back-in-stock/customer copy more SUGAR-like, and sharpen the glitter sell-through plan beyond one bundle.

strength: It takes apart the blended 4.0 ROAS correctly, shows that non-brand PMax is losing money, and puts the pointed-flat price mismatch first.
mistake: The forecast leans a little optimistic on brand search absorbing nearly all brand value at much lower spend.
to10: Make the forecast a bit more conservative and add clearer week 2-4 budget reallocation rules by campaign and ROAS threshold.

strength: It gives a strong profit view, a sensible budget split, and useful stop rules for the following weeks.
mistake: It does not isolate PMax without brand as clearly, and the title example feels more keyword-stuffed and less Rothy's than it should.
to10: Lead with the PMax-without-brand ROAS, make the title and ad copy warmer and more customer-led, and avoid platform-risky directions like simply removing PMax image and video assets.

strength: It acts on the three real levers in the data: the silent delivery gap, low fit finder use for bras, and the refund-first portal.
mistake: A few customer-facing lines could be softened slightly, and the swap-sales number is an upper bound that needs clearer caveats.
to10: Tighten the customer copy a little more to feel fully Lounge, and show the swap impact as a range net of likely exchange behaviour rather than a headline maximum.

strength: It gives a clear first move and gets the core maths right, especially on tickets, bra returns and swaps keeping sales rather than saving return cost.
mistake: It misses the proactive day-3 update, weakens the portal nudge by not pre-selecting size swap, and some copy sounds too certain about delivery timing.
to10: Add the day-3 reassurance message, make size swap the default for fit reasons while keeping refund visible, and rewrite delivery copy so it gives a range without sounding like a promise.

strength: It acts on the main signals: brings back the pause for busy learners, stops discounting trip-over users, and treats lack of progress as a reminder/product problem.
mistake: The revenue range and the switch/reminder assumptions need a little tightening before reporting as a forecast.
to10: Tighten the forecast language and test plan, especially for the untested annual-plan switch and reminder offer.

strength: It is buildable, clear, and correctly makes the paused busy-user path the biggest priority.
mistake: It reintroduces the 50% discount for app switchers without evidence, and then appears to count that discounted revenue at full value.
to10: Remove the unsupported discount path, fix the discounted revenue maths, and keep the save offers focused on pause, annual switch, and reminder setup.

strength: It catches the main signals in the data and turns them into three clear, publishable articles in the right voice.
mistake: It recommends merging the already-helpful payment article and gives a point forecast that is a bit too confident, with some assumed product details around restoring deleted expenses.
to10: Drop the unnecessary payment-article merge, make the forecast a clear range, and verify or soften the restore/undelete product claims.

strength: It ranks the work by ticket reduction, explains the hidden causes plainly, and gives an honest forecast range with clean working.
mistake: The articles are slightly less ready to publish because one includes visible meta text like “Search words,” and it misses the future in-app link from currency screens to the currency article.
to10: Remove the meta notes from the customer-facing article, add the currency-screen link once live, and add a little more exact step detail where available.

strength: It gives the right strategic answer with strong maths: do not cut to 20%, protect the top 20, extend credit to 90 days, and fix payouts fast.
mistake: The 40% first-year Partner tier adds cost just as the plan is trying to reassure finance, and the free account promise is not fully costed.
to10: Tighten the Partner tier economics and make clear whether the 40% uplift is a test, a cap, or only for selected top partners.

strength: It focuses the plan exactly where the data points: keep 30%, fix attribution and payouts, and spend the $40,000 on the small group that already drives the programme.
mistake: It could give the top Partner tier a slightly more distinctive benefit beyond support and grants, since the rival still looks better in year-one cash.
to10: Add one stronger non-commission Partner benefit for the top 20, such as co-marketed launches or priority feature access, with a clear owner and cap.

strength: It answers the brief exactly: re-carton first, rush only the top 5 shades, stay inside ₹1.2 crore, and gives an honest back-in-stock line in brand voice.
mistake: It spends about ₹1.187 crore with only ₹1.3 lakh spare, a thin buffer if freight or unit costs shift slightly.
to10: Show the exact per-shade split and the warehouse calendar for the re-cartoning run, so the ops lead can start Monday morning without any further maths.

strength: Reserve rule and per-shade reorder points show good planning discipline, and it keeps a sensible ₹4.07 lakh cash reserve.
mistake: It invents a 'Night-out kit' and a SKU bundle without owner sign-off, and its pre-order copy promises a ship date it cannot guarantee, which breaks the honesty principle.
to10: Drop the invented bundle, use only the owner's real lines, and lock every promise to a date the rush order actually supports.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even and puts the feed fix first, with the customer's own words in the titles.
mistake: Its projection table quietly assumes brand search jumps to about 25 ROAS and PMax recovers to 2.6, which flatters the base case and undercuts the 'judge by profit' message.
to10: Show the expected profit range from cautious to base with the assumptions on one line each, so the owner can see the upside is not guaranteed.

strength: Uses only the owner's own numbers, gives a profit range instead of a single promise, and adds stop rules that protect the brand if the switch goes wrong.
mistake: The 106-character title exceeds Google's 150 limit only in theory, but its length and order bury the searched words late and read more like keyword stuffing than the warm brand voice.
to10: Tighten the title to the searched words first in the brand's warm, plain voice, and keep the A/B test rule.

strength: It nails all three levers from my data (silent days 3-5, fit finder hidden, refund-first portal) and writes each message in our voice with one button and an honest expected range.
mistake: Message 2 asking a first-time buyer to 'change it on the result page before we pack' depends on an unproven 'orders can be changed until packed' assumption, which risks a broken promise if the warehouse can't hold orders.
to10: Tighten the copy so every line is grade 6-7 and drop or soften the change-before-packing line into a safer 'reply if you need a different size' fallback.

strength: The fit-check copy is practical and body-positive ('band on the loosest hook', 'comfort beats the number on the tag'), and the hold-out advice is sensible.
mistake: The swap saving of 'up to £183,800' assumes every extra swap is a £58 order, which inflates the headline number I'd quote to my team.
to10: Ground the swap saving in a realistic per-swap value (as o1 does at 1,300-2,240 kept orders) and make the day-3 message a clear value-add rather than a status update.

strength: Gives a straight, well-evidenced no to the 20% cut and builds the whole plan around the top-20 creator educators, the 90-day window and faster payouts, with the maths traceable.
mistake: The perk table spend figures are a little tight and the $52/month Podia plan price is assumed, which finance may query; also the 'Creator educators' section could say more about what Renee hears.
to10: Tie each first-30-days action to the one partner manager's actual hours and make the $40,000 perk costs unarguable.

strength: The straight answer, the 31% first-year maths for the Partner tier, and the crisp one-page rules and 30-day plan make this immediately runnable, and the voice is genuinely Podia.
mistake: The Partner tier at 40% for 12 months is richer than needed and its $46,000 cost plus $63,000 window cost plus content fund risks eating the saving the owner wanted to protect; the break-even 'four people' line mixes lifetime and annual revenue slightly.
to10: Prove the 40%-for-12-months Partner tier is affordable within the $40,000 perk budget and the 30% overall commission envelope.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart line by line against the 2.5 break-even, shows non-brand Google lost about $20,000, and proves it with a segment table that adds exactly to $144,960.
mistake: No concrete ad copy or feed attribute work (size, colour, material, highlights), so the customer's words only appear in one title line rather than in headlines and feed fields.
to10: Add ready-to-paste search headlines and descriptions in Claire's and Nina's own words, plus the missing feed fields (size, colour, material, highlights), without losing the per-line profit ranges.

strength: Sharp, on-brand execution: customer-language headlines and a gentle target-ROAS ramp (2.6 then 3.0) so PMax does not stall after the brand exclusion.
mistake: The base case leans on brand search turning $18,000 into $455,000 (ROAS ~25) versus $204,000 from $12,000 last month, and the cautious case never stress-tests that single assumption that carries 40% of projected value.
to10: Show brand-search value as a defensible range instead of a 95%-retention leap, and pull bags out of PMax so the scaled bags campaign is not bidding against itself.

strength: One costed, unmistakable first move this week (dispatch email at warehouse exit, courier-scan email switched off), with every projection traced back to her numbers and given as a range.

to10: Add the morning-of-day-3 status email to carry the ticket claim, and put real fit guidance in the post-delivery bra message instead of only a swap nudge.

strength: Every signal gets its own mechanism: day-3 status email, reason-first portal that only pushes swaps on size, real fit guidance after delivery, and a weekly reason feed back to product pages.
mistake: The refund share falling from 82% to 65% and the £183,800 'sales kept' figure have no stated basis, and there is no message for a parcel that never turns up.
to10: Ground the swap assumption (or widen it to 70-75% like the other ranges) and add a 'running late' email for parcels that miss the window.

strength: Reason-by-reason splitting (monthly vs annual, reminder set vs not) with every number traced and an honest low-end range from the pause alone, plus a 'Bad news' section that names the billing dependency before I find it.

to10: Add the confirmation screens for pause, switch and reminder, show the working behind the top of the range, and the sprint could start Monday with no gaps.

strength: It gives every outcome its own confirmation screen and adds a 10% holdout against today's flow, which is the one thing I would want to see added to any version of this plan.
mistake: The money has sloppy seams an owner would catch: £607 labelled 'after discount' when it is full-price treatment, 'about 173 in the new flow' conflated with acceptors, and a £136,000 'per monthly group' figure that overstates, and there is no honest range.
to10: Fix the value labels, add a range with the low end derived from the pause alone, and put the build notes in the order to do them (pause in billing first).

strength: The three articles are genuinely publishable, covering both app and web paths (including how to cancel the next Pro payment), and it turns the 4,900 no-click searches into a concrete search-synonym fix plus a contextual 'Balances are simplified. Why?' link on the balances screen.
mistake: It merges a well-performing article ('Recording a payment', 71% helpful) for little gain and gives a single point estimate rather than the honest range the owner asked for, though it does show a half-share downside.
to10: Turn the forecast into a proper range as the headline, drop the low-value merge, and state the 18,000 x $4.10 = $73,800 monthly baseline so the saving has a denominator.

strength: Calibrating the forecast band to today's 'Did this help?' rates (25-50%, below the 38-71% actuals) is the sharpest reasoning on the page, and the decision line plus 'nothing needs merging' framing reads fast.

to10: Cut the contact CTAs from the top deflection articles, add the splitwise.com restore path, and give the Pro cancellation its exact steps so all three articles can ship untouched.

strength: It nails the real problem - top 5 matte shades run out ~1 Dec, rush order lands 7 Dec - and builds every number, date and message around that gap, including the 6,400 held units as a day-one fix.
mistake: It orders 22,000 rush + 25,000 standard top-5 units where the brief's own demand math suggests less is needed, and the 6-day gap is handled but the reserve of only ₹1.3 lakh is thinner than the freight/overrun risk it names.
to10: Tighten the rush and standard quantities to the demand build (so nothing over-orders cash) and show the shade-level split arithmetic explicitly so the ops lead can place POs without guessing.

strength: It shows its working line by line - the 20,100-unit rush demand build, the reorder points, the Night-out kit margin - and turns dead stock into a sellable bundle with real economics.
mistake: It spends ₹115.93 lakh including a ₹0.38 lakh re-carton and leaves a ₹4.07 lakh reserve, but the standard top-5 order of 20,000 lands 28 Dec while the rush covers only to ~27 Dec, so any sale spike above 2.5x risks a second thin gap it doesn't flag.
to10: Flag the late-December handoff risk between rush and standard stock explicitly and give the owner a one-line "if this slips, do this" fallback.

strength: It takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even, puts the feed fix first, and moves the cut money to bags and the customer's own search words inside the fixed $240,000.
mistake: Some projections are optimistic and the reserve rule adds a layer of complexity the owner may not want in month one.
to10: Trim the projection table to two credible cases with the working shown and confirm the price-mismatch root cause before leaping to the target-ROAS change.

strength: Clean profit view by line and a strong feed diagnosis with the 15.6% of site revenue at stake.
mistake: It claims brand terms are 50% of value when the brief's numbers make it about 41% of PMax value and 50% only if you add brand search, which muddles the core insight; the base case ROAS 4.6 and profit jump look too rosy.
to10: Get the brand share right and make the projections conservative and traceable line by line.

strength: Every message is written and on-brand, and the numbers are traced to the data with honest ranges and a hold-out plan.
mistake: The '£183,800 in sales kept' figure overstates the swap value: it assumes every extra swap is a full £58 order saved, when many are single items and still incur the £7.50 cost.
to10: Tie the swap saving to the actual item value and net of the £7.50 handling cost, and show the working.

strength: The numbers are conservative and correctly net of costs, with a clear first move and a tight test-and-learn plan.
mistake: The fit check message is terse and missing the reassurance and free-swap clarity that would make Jess act; copy feels more like a template than a written message.
to10: Flesh out messages 2 and 5 with the same warm, one-button clarity and specific fit advice as the best answer, while keeping the tight numbers.

strength: A complete, buildable one-screen flow with reason-specific copy in Babbel's warm voice and 'Cancel my subscription' live throughout.
mistake: Gives a 50%-off price match to the 'switching apps' group, which contradicts the owner's annoyance at keeping the discount and spends margin on 8% who are already leaving for a rival.
to10: Drop or reframe the discount for switchers, tighten the revenue maths with an explicit per-group net-value range, and add a clean first-month tracking dashboard.

strength: Correctly kills the discount entirely, treats 'switching apps' as a clean exit, and puts the pause-rebuild as the first move with honest bad news and a range.
mistake: The headline '2,170' and range are slightly loose: the reminder group is barely defensible and the 'if switch and reminder do as well as the pause' range is a stretch the owner may not buy.
to10: Tighten the revenue range to the tested pause-only floor plus a clearly labelled upside, and add a one-line first-month scorecard with the one metric that matters (kept at 90 days by reason).

strength: It nails every signal in the data — Simplify debts split out, the 4,900 no-click searches, the 2,000 Apple/Google refunds — and turns them into three publish-ready articles plus a ticket forecast with real working and a down-side range.
mistake: It still tells people to turn Simplify debts off to see who owes whom, which changes the view for the whole group and risks new confusion; a safer article would show the per-expense view without flipping the group setting.
to10: Drop the group-wide Simplify toggle advice in favour of a per-expense view, and confirm the in-app button names before publishing so the steps are exactly right.

strength: It reads fastest of the two — bad news in three lines, a tight priority table, articles that answer in the first sentence, and a transparent 25%–50% range with the maths shown.
mistake: It says 'you can restore deleted expenses from Activity' as fact without telling people to check that the Restore option exists on their version, and its 'Contact us' fallbacks lean on a form the owner may not have wired up.
to10: Add the web version of the restore steps and a one-line check that the bold button names match the live app, so the articles are genuinely publish-ready.

strength: Straight, numerically grounded answer on the 20% cut using lifetime value, plus a named top-20 focus and fixes to the window and payouts that match the data signals exactly.

to10: Tighten the payout maths and show the work under the '12.5% revenue drop' break-even so every number traces cleanly.

strength: The 40%-for-12-months Partner tier plus a costed 31% first-year revenue estimate is a genuinely fresh, defensible option that beats the rival on year-one pay without blanket cost.

to10: Pin down the 90-day window cost with a shown calculation and reconcile every perk to the $40,000 so the budget is airtight.

strength: It proves non-brand Google lost about $20,000 last month, puts every segment against the 2.5 break-even, and spots that the 1.2 on broad 'women's flats' is partly the 212 missing sizes, so it trims rather than kills it.

strength: The feed and title sections are the most complete of the two, with structured-data checks, sale_price for promos, variant links, size and highlight fields, and ad copy built from Claire's and Nina's own words.

strength: A tight, owner-ready package with a today-vs-expected summary table at the top, named owners per task, and honest, traceable numbers (e.g. swap sales kept of £75.7k-£129.7k rather than a rosy headline).

to10: Add a low-cost proactive day-3 'nearly there, nothing to do' touch to catch the 62% ticket spike in its window, and note that the day-5 late email comes too late to prevent most tickets.

strength: Best mechanism for the ticket problem: a proactive day-3 email+SMS inside the spike window, plus specific fit guidance (band on loosest hook, snug and level) and size reasons fed back to product pages.

to10: Replace the £183,800 headline with a realistic cost-saved and honest swap-sales range (like £58 per item, not per order) and add named owners per workstream so it can be handed straight to the team.

strength: Every branch is finished — the six reason labels, the offer card, the done screen and the email confirmation — plus logging and a 10% holdout, so the product team can build it next sprint without another meeting.
mistake: It keeps a speculative 50% discount for switchers with no test behind it and then books that group at £607 'after discount' when 67 subscribers at half price is about £300, and it gives no honest range as I asked.

strength: It leads with the decision and the billing blocker, puts 'rebuild the pause this week' first, and backs the headline with a +930 to +2,740 range and a clean reason-by-reason table that matches my splits exactly.

to10: Write the done screen and confirmation email for each accepted offer, spell out the six reason labels, and tie the high end of the range to the stated accept rate.

strength: The three articles are genuinely publishable tomorrow - the restore article covers both app and web, the refund article includes cancellation steps, and the forecast shows per-topic working with a stated downside.

strength: It leads with a decision and an honest 11%-22% range, justifies the 25%-50% band against today's 'Did this help?' rates, and correctly says nothing needs merging - the problem is articles hiding the answer.

strength: It names the re-cartoning job as the Monday task, rushes only the top 5 matte shades, and keeps the whole order inside ₹1.2 crore with a dated ops calendar.

strength: It explains the gap honestly, protects bridal artists like Farah with a pro pre-order, and turns the glitter palette into a party-season price and bundle plan with dates.

strength: Takes apart the 4.0 ROAS, leads with the feed fix, and delivers a budget split that adds to exactly $240,000 with profit, not just ROAS, as the yardstick.

strength: Clean, honest decomposition showing brand terms are 11% of spend and 50% of value, with PMax ex-brand losing ~$36,700, and a ready-to-paste title and feed checklist.

strength: Ties every message, portal change and timing back to the three cost pools (silence, fit, refunds) with a clear week-by-week order and the cheapest fix first.

strength: The numbers are honest and internally consistent, especially the note that a swap still costs the £7.50 and the cautious swap-sales range, plus the 'running late' message that goes beyond day-5 silence.

strength: Reads the data the way the owner does: leads with Simplify debts inside the balances article, retitles the delete article using the exact no-click searches, and tells app-store refunders where to go first.

strength: The clearest owner-facing document: an upfront decision with an honest 11%-22% range, a tight 'bad news first' framing, and articles that answer in the first two lines without burying the reader.

strength: It gives the straight no on the 20% cut with the lifetime value maths, then ties the tier design, 90-day window and payout fixes directly to the named data signals (58% credited to no one, 41-day median, top-20 concentration).

strength: Flawlessly integrates the specific customer quotes into the titles and ad copy while nailing every mathematical and budget constraint.

strength: Provides a very clear, workable UI flow with exact copy that aligns nicely with the brand guidelines.

strength: Perfectly synthesizes the data and business constraints, putting the most critical blocker—the billing system—front and center while delivering an honest projection range.

strength: Provides a very clear table of actions with specific reasons, timelines, and accurate math for the ticket forecast.

strength: Follows all instructions flawlessly, weaving the exact brand phrase seamlessly into the first article and providing a realistic ticket drop range upfront.

strength: Rock-solid mathematical breakdown of the coverage gap, clear Monday PO schedule, and an ongoing weekly reorder framework.
mistake: Missed the specific behavioral risks of bridal makeup artists like Farah, missing a chance to tailor order caps or pro allocations.
to10: Incorporate specific tactics for high-volume bridal kit buyers like Farah alongside Tanvi to prevent bulk stock wiping before the sale.

strength: Directly integrates customer personas into operations by creating pro pre-orders for Farah and capping online cart quantities to protect Tanvi.

strength: Immediately dismantles the deceptive 4.0 ROAS against the 2.5 break-even threshold and crafts flawless customer-facing ad copy tailored to Claire.

to10: Add concrete rollback and cut thresholds for PMax performance during weeks 2 to 4.

strength: Superior tactical execution details, including removing bags from PMax listing groups to stop cannibalization and providing explicit stop-rules for weeks 2 to 4.

strength: The proactive Day 3 check-in directly solves the Day 3–5 silence driving 62% of WISMO tickets, paired with superb, body-neutral bra-fitting guidance in the delivery email.

strength: Strong executive summary table right at the top and a clever nod to Amira's gifting use-case in Message 5.

strength: Excellent segmentation of cancel reasons with mathematically sound projections that properly price 12-month switchers at the discounted rate.

strength: Directly provides the requested projection range, moves post-cancel trip reminders to the confirmation screen to keep the save flow friction-free, and drafts the critical pre-restart email.

strength: Captures every detail of the brief, incorporates our exact brand phrase ('Here\'s who owes what, and why'), and makes the sharp call not to merge working articles.

strength: Great multi-platform guidance (iOS, Android, and web) in the copy, plus a smart in-app UX recommendation for simplified balances.

strength: Flawless arithmetic on lifetime values and churn, paired with a sharp, realistic budget where software accounts are given at zero marginal cost so cash goes directly into creator content.

strength: Translates the specific customer personas into a brilliant order-capping and pro pre-order strategy to stretch scarce inventory.

strength: Accurately calculates the exact unit gap during the stock-out window to correctly size the rush order buffer.

strength: The masterfully constructed profit table that deconstructs the entire account into a single view, paired with expert-level technical execution (removing bags from PMax so Standard Shopping can actually scale).

strength: Flawlessly translates the data into perfectly timed interventions, notably the day-3 tracking update and targeting the fit email strictly at first-time bra buyers.
